messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo is a 28-year-old Latino man who works as a corrections officer at a state prison. He was referred for psychological evaluation following a period of escalating interpersonal conflict at work and at home. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 42 and describes a significant deterioration in functioning over the past several months, tracing everything back to the sudden death of his younger brother, Rodrigo, who died in a car accident without warning. There had been no illness, no goodbye. Mateo had been the last family member to speak to him by phone that evening, and when the call ended, he had thought nothing of it. He has not been able to stop thinking about it since.

In the weeks following Rodrigo's death, Mateo began to notice that ordinary moments could pull him under without warning. A news segment about a family killed in a highway collision, a coworker mentioning that his father had passed — these were enough to produce a creeping sense of unreality, as though the floor beneath him had quietly disappeared. In those moments, Mateo would feel himself beginning to detach, watching his own hands from somewhere slightly outside his body. When that dissociative feeling came on, he found himself reaching up to cover his face with both hands, pressing his palms hard against his eyes as though he could physically block the sensation from taking hold. He also began steering sharply away from anything connected to grief or loss — he stopped attending church, where the priest sometimes spoke about the dead, and he avoided the corner of the break room where colleagues had placed a memorial photo for a recently deceased inmate. These avoidances were not planned; they accumulated the way scar tissue does, quietly and without announcement.

What made the triggers especially unbearable was what they confirmed for him. Mateo had come to believe, with a certainty that felt almost physical, that he had failed Rodrigo. He had been the older brother. He should have known something was wrong. He should have kept him on the phone longer, driven to see him, done something. This conviction — that he had failed to protect someone who depended on him — sat at the centre of his self-understanding and darkened everything around it. He was certain he had been a happy person once, but that version of himself now seemed like someone else entirely, a stranger he could no longer locate. Worse, he saw no path forward. When he tried to imagine the future, he found nothing — not despair exactly, but a kind of blankness, as though the years ahead had simply been removed.

These appraisals did not stay still. They fed back into the very triggers he was trying to escape. When Mateo found himself believing he had no future, the world began to feel thin and unreal in a way that made dissociative episodes more likely to surface — a low-grade fragility that meant almost any reference to loss could tip him over. And the strategies he had adopted to manage the pain were making things worse in ways he was only beginning to acknowledge. Picking arguments with his wife or manufacturing tension with colleagues at the prison gave him a few minutes of sharp, present-tense feeling that cut through the numbness — but when the drama subsided, he was left more depleted than before, the grief sitting heavier, and the belief that he was broken and beyond repair slightly more entrenched. Covering his face and walking away from reminders kept the worst moments at bay in the short term, but they also meant he never processed anything, and the appraisals calcified further. The avoidance itself, over time, began to sensitise him — ordinary stimuli that might once have passed unnoticed now carried a faint charge of threat, making the dissociative feeling easier to trigger.

At the prison, where death and loss are structural features of the environment, Mateo finds it nearly impossible to escape reminders entirely. A news broadcast playing in the staff lounge, a conversation among inmates about a family member who died — these are daily occurrences he cannot avoid, and each one costs him something.

What finally brought him to seek help was his wife telling him, quietly, that she did not recognise him anymore. What he fears most is that she is right.
